title: Children-First Tree Walk
statement:
Given the root of a binary tree, list its values in post-order: for every node, first everything in its left subtree, then everything in its right subtree, and only then the node itself.

Return the values as an array. An empty tree gives [].

Recursion makes this short. Be ready for the follow-up: do it with your own stack instead.

examples.why: Both children of 2 come before 2, the whole left subtree comes before the right one, and the root 4 comes last.
1 has only a right child 2, and 2 has a left child 3. The deepest node is listed first.
Left child, right child, then the parent. Simply reversing the root-first order would give [3, 2, 1], which is wrong.

hints: Write the definition as a function: post-order(left), post-order(right), then the node.
Without recursion, try a different walk: node, right, left is easy with a stack, like a root-first walk with the children pushed in the other order. How does that relate to post-order?
Node-right-left, reversed, is left-right-node. Or keep one stack and a pointer to the last node you output, so you know when a node's right subtree is finished.

explain.intuition:
Post-order means a node is written only after both of its subtrees are done. That is the order you need whenever a parent depends on its children: freeing memory, summing folder sizes, or unmounting a component tree, where children clean up before their parent.

The iterative version has a neat shortcut. A root-first walk that visits the right child before the left one produces node, right, left. Reverse that list and you get left, right, node, which is exactly post-order. Pushing the left child first means the right one is popped first. The alternative, a single stack plus a "last output" pointer, avoids the reversal: a node on top of the stack is output only if it has no right child or its right child was the last thing output.
steps: If root is null, return []. Otherwise push it on a stack.
Pop a node and append its value to out.
Push its left child, then its right child (if they exist), so the right one is popped next.
Repeat until the stack is empty.
pitfalls: Reversing an ordinary root-first walk (node, left, right). That gives right, left, node, as the third example shows.
In the one-stack version, popping a node before its right subtree is finished. Track the last output node to tell "coming back from the left" from "coming back from the right".
Relying on recursion for a chain of tens of thousands of nodes, which can overflow the call stack.

complexity.space: O(n) for the output, O(h) to O(n) for the stack

solutions.title: Recursion
solutions.idea: Left subtree, right subtree, then the node, exactly as defined.

solutions.title: Reversed node-right-left walk
solutions.idea: A stack walk that visits node, right, left is easy; reversing its output gives left, right, node.

solutions.title: One stack and the last output node
solutions.idea: Walk left pushing nodes. Output the top only when its right subtree is empty or was just finished; otherwise go right first.

followups: Delete every node of a tree, freeing children before parents, without recursion.
